why_this_tool: pandas shows every stage of the cleanup, from missing-value handling to match keys and survivorship, as plain inspectable tables on a laptop, so you see exactly what each rule does to each record.
alternatives: Splink does probabilistic linkage with trained match weights on a SQL backend, OpenRefine is a point-and-click tool for clustering and cleanup, DuckDB runs the same profiling and joins as in-process SQL over files, and Apache Spark spreads the same logic across a cluster when an extract will not fit on one machine.

setup.do: Create a fresh Python virtual environment, install pandas at one pinned version, record that version in a requirements file, and build a tiny DataFrame from a dictionary to confirm the install.
setup.done_when: A three-row DataFrame prints in your Python session and the requirements file names one exact pandas version.
setup.why: A pinned version keeps missing-value and dtype behaviour the same on every rerun. The constructor is the entry point for everything that follows.

setup.do: Write two small overlapping customer extracts by hand, one shaped like a CRM export and one like an ERP export, of about thirty rows each, with repeated customers, blank cells, placeholder words such as unknown, and inconsistent phone and date formats.
setup.done_when: Two files exist on disk and you have a written list of which rows are true duplicates and which cells are really missing.

source.title: Working with missing data — pandas 3.0.6 documentation

setup.why: You need data whose flaws you planted yourself so you can check that each later step finds them. Knowing what pandas counts as missing tells you which flaws it will miss at first.

setup.do: Install the optional pyarrow package into the same environment and pin it too, so Arrow-backed column types are available.
setup.done_when: A Series created with an Arrow-backed string type prints its dtype without an import error.
setup.why: Arrow-backed types give strings and integers one consistent missing marker. You will rely on that when comparing fields across sources.

steps.do: Load both extracts into DataFrames with every column read as text, then inspect shape, column names, dtypes and the first rows of each.
steps.done_when: You can state the row count, column count and dtype of every column for both extracts.
steps.why: Reading everything as text stops pandas from guessing types and silently mangling identifiers and postcodes. This first look is the start of profiling an unknown extract.

steps.do: Run isna over each extract and compute the count and share of missing values per column, saving the result as a small profile table.
steps.done_when: A profile table lists each column with its missing count, and the counts are lower than the missing cells you planted because the placeholder words are not yet detected.
steps.why: A per-column missingness profile shows which fields can serve as match keys and which are too sparse to trust. It is also the baseline for every later comparison.

steps.do: Replace the placeholder tokens you planted, such as unknown, a lone dash and empty strings, with real missing values, then rerun the profile and compare it to the first one.
steps.done_when: The second profile shows higher missing counts that match the number of cells you planted as missing.

source.title: Working with missing data — pandas 3.0.6 documentation

steps.why: Customer exports hide missing data behind sentinel text, and pandas only treats it as missing after you convert it. The before and after profiles show how much was hidden.

steps.do: Run convert_dtypes on both cleaned extracts and compare the dtypes before and after.
steps.done_when: Identifier columns show a nullable integer or string dtype instead of object or float, and no identifier has gained a decimal point.
steps.why: Nullable dtypes keep integer identifiers as integers when values are missing and give every column the same missing marker. That makes later comparisons predictable.

steps.do: Write a source-to-target mapping spec as a table with one row per source column, giving its target name and target type. Add a crosswalk dictionary for coded values such as country and status codes, and apply both with rename and replace so the two extracts share one schema.
steps.done_when: Both DataFrames have identical column names and each coded column contains only values from the target code list.
steps.why: A written spec and crosswalk make the mapping reviewable by the customer and repeatable when a new export arrives. Applying the crosswalk through a dictionary keeps the lookup as data rather than scattered logic.

steps.do: Write regular expression replacements that normalize names, phone numbers and postcodes into a new set of columns: strip punctuation and repeated whitespace and remove legal suffixes. Keep the raw columns untouched.
steps.done_when: Rows you planted as the same customer now carry identical normalized name and phone values while their raw values still differ.

source.title: Working with missing data — pandas 3.0.6 documentation

steps.why: Normalization is what lets two spellings of the same entity compare as equal. Keeping the raw values beside the normalized ones keeps the work traceable.

steps.do: Configure dropna with a subset and a threshold so rows lacking every usable identifier go to a quarantine DataFrame instead of being deleted, and write down the rule you chose.
steps.done_when: The kept and quarantined row counts add up to the original row count.
steps.why: Records with nothing to match on cannot be resolved and will produce false links if left in. Quarantining rather than deleting keeps the decision reversible.

steps.do: Create a deterministic match key from the normalized fields and set it as the index of the stacked extracts. Run the duplicate label detection checks to list every key that appears more than once, and assign a cluster identifier to each group.
steps.done_when: The list of repeated keys covers the exact duplicates you planted, and each has one cluster identifier.
steps.why: Exact-key matching is the cheap, explainable first pass that resolves most duplicates. Detecting repeated keys on the index is how you find and count them.

steps.do: Compare a missing match field against another missing match field and against a real value, and record what each comparison returns.
steps.done_when: You can show that comparing two missing values yields missing rather than true, and you have written the rule your linkage will use for that case.

verified.section_found: Propagation in arithmetic and comparison operations#

steps.why: A missing value does not equal another missing value, so a naive comparison can neither confirm nor rule out a match. You must decide explicitly how missing fields contribute to a link.

steps.do: Create candidate pairs by joining the remaining unmatched records to each other on a blocking key such as postcode. Compute per-field agreement columns, then use where to turn each agreement into a positive weight, each disagreement into a negative weight and each missing comparison into zero. Sum the weights and pick a threshold.
steps.done_when: A pair table shows a total score per candidate pair, the planted fuzzy duplicates score above your threshold and unrelated pairs in the same block score below it.
steps.why: Blocking keeps the number of comparisons manageable and match weights let strong fields count for more than weak ones. This is the core of probabilistic record linkage, and building it by hand shows what a dedicated linkage library automates.

steps.do: Create one golden record per cluster by ordering the sources by trust and filling each missing field from the next most trusted source. Save a crosswalk table that links every source row identifier to its golden identifier and the rule that merged it.
steps.done_when: The golden table has one row per cluster with fewer missing cells than any single source, and you can pick any golden row and list the source rows behind it.
steps.why: Survivorship rules decide which value wins when sources disagree. The crosswalk lets you explain any golden value and undo a wrong merge.

steps.do: Configure the golden table to disallow duplicate labels on its golden identifier index, then try to append a row with an existing identifier and confirm the operation fails.
steps.done_when: Adding a repeated golden identifier raises an error instead of producing a second row.
steps.why: A golden record set is only trustworthy if one identifier means one entity. An enforced invariant catches a bad merge when it happens instead of in a downstream feature.

steps.do: Write the whole pipeline as one script that runs in the pinned environment from the raw files to the golden table and crosswalk. Add explicit isna-based checks that stop the run when a required field is missing or a missing count exceeds the profiled baseline, then run it twice.
steps.done_when: Two consecutive runs produce identical golden and crosswalk outputs, and blanking a required field in the input makes the run stop with a clear message.

source.title: Working with missing data — pandas 3.0.6 documentation

steps.why: A missing value cannot be used directly as a true or false condition, so automated checks must test for it explicitly. A pinned, rerunnable script with failing checks is the closest laptop equivalent to a production data job.
